extracted.intended_audience: general readers, mathematicians and computer scientists interested in computer-assisted proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Overview of methods, philosophical objections, and practical standards for producing and validating computer-assisted mathematical proofs (including rigorous numerics, proof assistants, and strategies for gaining confidence in computational results).

rubrics_metrics.name: Validated numerics / rigorous numerics
rubrics_metrics.description: Computing numerically yet with mathematical rigour by using set-valued arithmetic and the inclusion principle so that the set-valued output of a numerical program encloses the solution of the original mathematical problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control, enclose and propagate round-off and truncation errors (for example via interval arithmetic). Reduce computation to elementary operations and replace numbers with intervals, performing elementary operations between such intervals to obtain provable bounds on results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-surveyability / verifiability
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer-assisted proofs should be human-surveyable so that mathematicians can, at least in principle, verify the logical steps; lack of surveyability is a core philosophical objection (Tymoczko) to lengthy computer-assisted proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article contrasts proofs that are human-surveyable (e.g., some interactive proof assistant outputs) with lengthy proofs-by-exhaustion that involve so many logical steps they are not practically verifiable by humans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid blind trust in computational processes (program/runtime/hardware errors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be wary of replacing logical deduction from axioms with trust in empirical computational processes that can be affected by errors in the computer program, runtime environment, and hardware.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a philosophical and practical concern motivating additional verification steps (see program correctness, replication, formal checking).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal verification / proof of program correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a formal proof of correctness for the computer program used in the proof so that the program's use can be regarded as verification rather than an empirical trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes this approach was successfully applied to the four color theorem (2005) and is presented as a way to resolve concerns about program errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replication across implementations
rubrics_metrics.description: Replicate computational results using different programming languages, different compilers, and different computer hardware to increase confidence in the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replication across independent implementations helps mitigate the risk of bugs or hardware-specific faults producing incorrect results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generate machine-readable reasoning and independent proof checking
rubrics_metrics.description: Produce the reasoning steps in machine-readable form and use a proof checker program to demonstrate correctness; validating a proof is easier than finding it, so checkers are simpler than the original assistant program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a simpler checker to validate machine-readable proofs can increase confidence, though skeptics may view this as adding complexity rather than restoring human understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove validity of the proof algorithm (treat algorithm as verified verifier)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove that the proof-generating algorithm itself is valid; if the algorithm is proved correct, then running it can be regarded as verification rather than as producing an empirical result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This perspective reframes some computer-assisted work as 'calculations' whose correctness rests on a proved algorithm rather than trusting ad-hoc computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer interactive proof assistants for human-readable formal verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Use interactive proof assistants that allow development of human-readable proofs which are nonetheless formally verified for correctness; such proofs are generally human-surveyable and avoid some controversies associated with proofs-by-exhaustion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interactive assistants (proof assistants) can produce formally checked proofs that balance machine verification with human readability; the Robbins conjecture example is cited as a case where surveyability remains challenging but better than exhaustive computational proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical insight and elegance as a quality consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether a computer-aided proof provides mathematical elegance, new insights, or useful concepts; lack of such insight is given as an argument against the value of some computer-aided proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes critics argue that lengthy proofs-by-exhaustion (computer-aided or not) may lack insight, and this aesthetic/epistemic criterion is part of the philosophical debate over the role of computers in mathematics.
